title: Can manually closing a page inside Puppeteer Cluster cause TargetCloseError with Firefox BiDi?
body:
I'm using Puppeteer Cluster 0.25.0 with Puppeteer Core 24.30.0 and Firefox WebDriver BiDi on Linux.

My cluster uses CONCURRENCY_CONTEXT, with maxConcurrency: 4 and retryLimit: 0.

During separate higher-concurrency experiments, I intermittently encountered errors including:

TargetCloseError: script.callFunction: Target closed

I noticed that my worker cleanup also explicitly closed the page supplied by Puppeteer Cluster.

Here is a simplified excerpt of the original pattern:

const cluster = await Cluster.launch({
  puppeteer,
  concurrency: Cluster.CONCURRENCY_CONTEXT,
  maxConcurrency: 4,
  retryLimit: 0,
  puppeteerOptions: {
    browser: 'firefox',
    protocol: 'webDriverBiDi',
    headless: true,
    executablePath: firefoxPath
  }
});

await Promise.all(jobs.map(job =>
  cluster.execute(job, async ({ page }) => {
    try {
      await processJob(page, job);
    } finally {
      await page.close();
    }
  })
));

await cluster.idle();
await cluster.close();

I understand that Puppeteer Cluster manages task resources internally. I've now removed the explicit page.close() from my actual runner and left page disposal to the cluster.

However, that change hasn't yet been verified against the original intermittent failure, so I can't say whether it resolves the error.

My question: Is manually closing the supplied page inside a cluster.execute() task unsupported or unsafe with CONCURRENCY_CONTEXT, particularly when using Firefox WebDriver BiDi?

I'm trying to establish the correct page-lifecycle ownership before investigating any remaining worker failures.

I've also reviewed the library's existing page-cleanup discussion in GitHub issue #34.

title: doxygen generation reports clang errors - how can I tell which file compilation triggered them?
body:
I'm using doxygen (v1.18.0) to generate documentation for a project of mine. Doxygen runs clang (or libclang) internally, on the various documented file, likely to collect items to document or figure out relations between entities; and - doxygen reports errors clang finds while running within/under doxygen, to it log or standard error stream. An error might look like:

error: /path/to/file.hpp:37:21: error: implicit instantiation of undefined 
template 'mylib::traits<foo>' [clang]

The thing is, it might be the case that when I compile my code the way my build system does, this problem will not manifest; and one needs to figure out which file was the 'root' for this compilation, to understand what got included (and in which order), and thus how we got the error or warning. Yet - by default, the doxygen log does not tell us that, i.e. we get all clang errors and warnings in sequence without prelude lines saying "invkoing clang on path/to/another_file.hpp".

My question: Is it possible to determine this information? i.e. which file doxygen was working on / invoking clang for, when a given clang warning or error was triggered?

Note: In this question, I don't care about errors or warnings reported by doxygen itself, separately from the clang invocation.

When building a React Progressive Web App (PWA), loading different dub tracks from YouTube involves a technical challenge: the official YouTube IFrame API does not provide native methods to switch or query multi-language audio (MLA) tracks programmatically via JavaScript.

Because YouTube serves adaptive streams and strictly signs media fragments (which requires a JavaScript engine to extract), you cannot safely fetch raw MLA files natively inside browser-side React code. You will need a backend API or a Serverless function (Node.js/Express) to interface with the PWA.

  • yt-dlp-exec (Node.js wrapper): This open-source wrapper allows you to trigger yt-dlp commands via a Node backend. Your React application makes a fetch request to your server, which executes yt-dlp --list-audio-tracks to return available language codes to the React PWA state.
  • fluent-ffmpeg: Once your backend uses yt-dlp to extract the desired dub track, you can stream it using fluent-ffmpeg to compress and re-encode it to a lightweight PWA-friendly audio format (like AAC or WebM) for the client application.

title: Ad-hoc, temporary print-based debugging Rust code without new type constraints
body:
Suppose I have some Rust code like

fn foo<T>(x: T) {
  // Complicated function.
}

fn function_that_calls_foo_to_honor_the_request_in_comments<T>(x: T) {
   foo(x)
}

that is called from a gazillion places all over my codebase.

Suppose, then, that I realize that something is wrong deep within foo. Sometimes, I might want to do some quick print-based debugging within the function. That would entail printing Ts with e.g. Debug formatting. Somewhere in the actual program being debugged, there are concrete instances of foo<T>, say e.g. foo<i64>. Since i64 implements Debug, I can easily add debugging print statements to foo<T> that would work for that particular monomorphization. However, since foo<T> is completely generic in T as it stands, the typechecker naturally demands that I restrict T: Debug. That would be OK to do temporarily and locally for debugging, except foo<T> is used in a gazillion places all over the code, so now all those sites need to get T: Debug too, which would be a real hassle to add and then remove. In the example above, imagine there are 100 more functions like function_that_calls_foo_to_honor_the_request_in_comments<T> and having to add the T: Debug constraint to all of them, and then remove that again after the debugging session.

Question: Is there a quick and dirty way to, for temporary debugging purposes only, add print statements to foo<T> that essentially say "if you're in a monomorphized version where T: Debug, perform these prints involving some Ts, otherwise don't (you can even exit or crash, I don't care)"?

I know that Rust is not geared for run-time type introspection, and I certainly don't propose using such mechanisms in general – I'm merely asking for a crude escape hatch for temporary debugging. I can envision something where there's a runtime check of the type name of T, and if it's say "i64" there's some transmutes into an i64 that's printed. I guess that would work, but maybe there's something a bit tidier?

Generally: I suppose the general question is "is there a way to tell the Rust compiler to do something as if a trait were satisfied even when the constraints don't promise it, and just die in a fireball if runtime reality doesn't match up?"

title: How do idioms like the Nifty Counter idiom work if even chars and char arrays have lifetimes?
body:
The Nifty Counter Idiom apparently is, or was, used for the std::cout object, and is used generally in order to ensure static objects are constructed before they're used, and destroyed after they're no longer going to be accessed. The gist of it something like this:

StreamInitializer::StreamInitializer ()
{
  if (nifty_counter++ == 0) new (&stream) Stream (); // placement new
}
StreamInitializer::~StreamInitializer ()
{
  if (--nifty_counter == 0) stream.~Stream ();
}

The constructor is placed in the header that is included before whatever object you're going to use, so that each place you use it you're guaranteed that the object has been constructed. Long story short, it's a reference counting mechanism to ensure lifetime in static object destruction and destruction between translation units.

The problem is as far as I see it, it involves storage buffer, in this particular example:

static typename std::aligned_storage<sizeof (Stream), alignof (Stream)>::type
  stream_buf; // memory for the stream object
Stream& stream = reinterpret_cast<Stream&> (stream_buf);

In other examples I've seen:

char buff[size];

Or any variant, but basically this is the storage where you object is constructed and destroyed. But doesn't this, the storage buffer itself, have a lifetime? I'm pretty sure it does, and it's destroyed during static destruction of static objects after main() has exited, and its order is not guaranteed or defined in any way. Doesn't this make this whole thing UB, with doing things like this:

if (--nifty_counter == 0) stream.~Stream ();

Where you're calling the destructor on possibly an already destroyed piece of memory, or for those pedantic of us, an area, or object (yes, chars are objects too as far as I know), whose lifetime has ended.

title: What is the difference between `std::launder(ptr)` and `reinterpret_cast<T*>(reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(ptr))` in C++29?
body:
In N5054, reinterpret_cast from integer to pointer is specified as ([expr.reinterpret.cast]):

A value of integral type or enumeration type can be explicitly converted to a pointer. If the value is one that can be produced by converting one or more pointer values to an integral type, the result is an unspecified choice among all such values that would result in the program having defined behavior. If no such value exists, the behavior is undefined.

Per P2414R12, this specification allows reinterpret_cast<T*>(reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(ptr)) to convert an invalid pointer value to a valid one, effectively updating pointer provenance. P2414R12 uses this expression to make atomic/volatile access to invalid pointer values well-formed.

It seems that std::launder(ptr) is also described as a provenance barrier, but its specification ([ptr.launder]) looks quite different.

I know that reinterpret_cast is not usable in constant expressions, but std::launder is. Other than that, is there any difference in effect between std::launder(ptr) and the reinterpret_cast approach?

For the reference, the new specification of reinterpret_cast is not from P2414R12, but from P2434R5. There's P3347R6 that seems related. All three papers are adopted in 2026-06.

title: How should I persist frequently updated in-memory state without blocking a high-frequency event-processing workflow?
body:
How can I safely persist frequently updated in-memory state without blocking a real-time workflow?

I'm building a real-time, event-driven workflow execution engine using Node.js/TypeScript, Redis, and PostgreSQL.

The engine processes continuous market-data stream ticks. Each workflow maintains a small set of variables whose latest values must be retained across consecutive ticks.

My primary requirement is fast in-memory variable access during workflow execution, while also providing reasonable recovery after a worker crash or restart.

Current architecture

  • Node.js worker: Processes incoming stream ticks sequentially for each workflow.

  • In-memory state: Holds workflow-scoped variables for fast reads and updates.

  • Redis: Available for caching, streams, and potential asynchronous persistence.

  • PostgreSQL: Stores persistent variables for recovery across worker restarts.

Ticks can arrive asynchronously at irregular intervals, and each tick may update only a subset of the variables.

For example:

Tick 1: counter = 10, risk = 0.5
Tick 2: counter = 20
Tick 3: risk = 0.7
Tick 4: reads counter = 20, risk = 0.7

Consistency requirement: Within a single running workflow worker, each tick must observe the latest variable values written by previously completed ticks.

A single workflow processes its ticks sequentially, so concurrent updates to the same variable within that worker are not currently expected.

Current implementation

Currently, when a variable changes, the engine:

  1. Evaluates the new variable value.

  2. Commits it to PostgreSQL.

  3. Invalidates the Redis cache.

  4. Updates the worker's in-memory state.

  5. Continues executing subsequent workflow nodes.

This provides durable updates but introduces database I/O into the execution path whenever a variable changes.

The performance concern

My concern is that synchronous database writes could introduce unnecessary latency when variables are updated frequently.

For example:

Tick 1: counter = 10
Tick 2: counter = 20
Tick 3: counter = 30
...
Tick 10000: counter = 10000

Persisting every intermediate value is unnecessary because only the latest value matters for subsequent workflow executions.

Even asynchronous writes could create a growing backlog if updates arrive faster than the persistence layer can process them.

Regarding actual performance measurements: I haven't yet established the peak tick rate or confirmed that PostgreSQL writes are a measurable bottleneck. This is currently an architectural concern, not a proven performance problem.

I plan to benchmark tick throughput, variable-update frequency, PostgreSQL write latency, and P95/P99 workflow execution times before changing the implementation.

Proposed approach: RAM-first with asynchronous checkpointing

I'm considering the following design:

  1. Update variables immediately in worker RAM.

  2. Track only the latest changed values using a dirty-variable map.

  3. Periodically flush a versioned snapshot to Redis.

  4. Allow a background worker to checkpoint the latest Redis snapshot to PostgreSQL.

  5. Restore the latest recoverable checkpoint when the workflow worker restarts.

For example:

Tick 1: counter = 10  → RAM
Tick 2: counter = 20  → RAM
Tick 3: counter = 30  → RAM

Background flush:
Redis: counter = 30

Later checkpoint:
PostgreSQL: counter = 30

This would avoid creating a separate persistence job for every tick.

Recovery and data-loss expectations

I understand that data which never reaches persistent storage cannot be recovered.

I'm willing to accept losing recent unflushed variable updates if the worker crashes.

My initial target is approximately 1–2 seconds of potential state loss under normal operating conditions, although this would need to be validated through testing.

I also understand that periodic checkpointing alone cannot guarantee a strict recovery window during Redis/PostgreSQL outages.

The goal is to recover the latest successfully persisted state, not every intermediate tick.

Specific technical problem

One concern is how to safely handle overlapping asynchronous checkpoints.

For example:

Worker RAM:
Version 10 → counter = 100
Version 11 → counter = 200

Redis write for version 10 starts.
Redis write for version 11 starts.

Version 11 finishes first.
Version 10 finishes later.

Without version checking, the older write could overwrite the newer value.

The same issue could occur when a background worker checkpoints Redis state to PostgreSQL.

My question

Assuming a single active writer per workflow, would using monotonically increasing snapshot versions with conditional Redis and PostgreSQL updates be sufficient to prevent older asynchronous checkpoints from overwriting newer state?

Are there important race conditions or recovery issues with this approach that I should account for?

I'm specifically interested in ensuring that the persisted state never moves backwards, while allowing the live workflow to continue reading and updating variables in RAM without waiting for database writes.

SELECT motor,time,temperature,SUM(CASE WHEN temperature > 85 AND LAG(temperature) OVER (PARTITION BY motor ORDER BY time) <= 85 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER (PARTITION BY motor ORDER BY time) AS incident_id FROM motor_samples ORDER BY time;

Msg: org.apache.iotdb.jdbc.IoTDBSQLException: 701: Cannot nest window functions or row pattern measures inside window function arguments

title: How to source and map XMLTV EPG data for event-based sports channels whose names and IDs change per match?
body:
I'm building a guide (EPG) importer for a live sports application. Channels come from an M3U playlist that is re-fetched on a schedule, and guide data comes from XMLTV. I match the two on tvg-id = XMLTV channel id.

That works for ordinary 24/7 channels. It fails for per-event entries, which make up most of the playlist (about 19,800 entries in about 280 groups, one group per league). A typical entry looks like this:

#EXTINF:-1 tvg-id="" group-title="NBA",NBA 03: Lakers vs Celtics @ 8:00 PM ET

The problems:

  1. tvg-id is empty or reused, and the title changes for every match, so there is no constant key to match against an XMLTV <channel id>.

  2. An entry only carries video around its event, so a linear-style guide with back-to-back programmes doesn't describe it.

  3. XMLTV files I have tested only contain the 24/7 channels, not these per-event entries.

What I have tried:

  • Matching on tvg-id: only works for the 24/7 channels.

  • Fuzzy-matching the entry title against XMLTV display-name: too many false matches between similarly named entries.

  • Parsing team names and start time out of the title with a regex: works until the playlist changes its title format.

My question:

For per-event entries, is it more robust to generate the XMLTV myself from a fixtures schedule (one <programme> per fixture) than to look for them in an existing XMLTV file? If so, what is a reliable way to key a fixture to a playlist entry when the only link is the free-text title?

title: Linux Kernel 6.19+ / 7.0 & SERVER-121912: Is disabling glibc rseq and patching isKernelVersionSafeForTCMallocPerCPUCache safe for production?
body:
We are running MongoDB in Kubernetes on worker nodes that were recently updated to newer Linux kernels (specifically Ubuntu 24.04 with AWS 7.0.0-1011-aws and Azure 7.0.0-1014-azure).

Upon host reboot, MongoDB (both 8.3.1 and the latest 8.3.11) immediately crashes on container startup with exit code 1:

{"s":"F", "c":"CONTROL", "id":12257600, "msg":"MongoDB cannot start: Linux kernel versions 6.19 and newer has a known incompatibility with this version of MongoDB. See https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-121912 for more information."}

The Root Cause Context

From SERVER-121912, we understand that the Linux kernel changed the Restartable Sequences (rseq) struct/ABI starting in 6.19+, which breaks the per-CPU caching path in the bundled version of TCMalloc. MongoDB's validateRseqKernelCompat() performs an upfront uname() release check (isKernelVersionSafeForTCMallocPerCPUCache) and immediately aborts if major >= 7 or (major == 6 && minor >= 19).

The Solution We Built

Because rolling back host OS kernels across managed cloud clusters is not always viable, we built a patched container image with two components:

  1. Disabled Glibc RSEQ: We inject ENV GLIBC_TUNABLES="glibc.pthread.rseq=0" into the container. This tells glibc to block thread registration for rseq, forcing TCMalloc to gracefully fall back to standard Per-Thread Caching (ThreadCache) instead of per-CPU caching.

  2. Bypassed Startup Guard: Because MongoDB’s uname() check aborts before taking the tunable into account, we patch the function _ZN5mongo41isKernelVersionSafeForTCMallocPerCPUCacheENS_10StringDataE to immediately return true (mov $1, %al; ret; nop).

Our Verification So Far

  • Using an LD_PRELOAD utsname interceptor to simulate kernel releases:

    • Unpatched mongo:8.3.11 + 7.0.0-1011-aws ➔ Crashes with Fatal ID 12257600.

    • Patched image + 7.0.0-1011-aws ➔ Starts up cleanly, initializes WiredTiger 12, passes connection health checks, and processes read/write workloads with 0 restarts.

    • Verified full backwards compatibility when tested against 5.15.0.

Reference to Community Discussions

We noticed this is related to the discussions in docker-library/mongo (Discussion #748 regarding TCMalloc rseq SIGSEGV crashes and Issue #765 regarding kernel 7.x startup blocks). While setting GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.pthread.rseq=0 is known to stabilize the allocator, MongoDB's upfront uname() check still prevents startup on modern cloud kernels (e.g. AWS 7.0.0-1011-aws, Azure 7.0.0-1014-azure).

Questions for the Community & MongoDB Engineers

Before we roll this out across our production fleet, we’d love to get feedback from anyone who has dealt with this:

  1. Allocators & Concurrency: Does forcing TCMalloc to use standard Per-Thread caching (ThreadCache) instead of per-CPU caching introduce any hidden fragmentation or lock-contention risks under modest-sized workloads (container limits ~256Mi - 2Gi)?

  2. WiredTiger Independence: Beyond TCMalloc's memory allocation, are there any other kernel subsystem dependencies or ABI assumptions in WiredTiger / MongoDB that conflict with Linux 6.19+ or 7.x kernels?

  3. Upstream Roadmap: Is there an official compile flag, configuration parameter, or upstream patch scheduled that will allow bypassing the rigid version check when rseq=0 is set?

Would appreciate any sanity checks or "green signals" from folks running MongoDB in similar modern kernel environments!

title: Polarion ALM SDK: "Setting null owner twice!" when adding 2+ new Work Items to an existing Live Document in one transaction/revision
body:
I'm writing a custom Polarion ALM extension (OSGi plugin extending com.polarion.portal.tomcat.webapps, Polarion version 3.25.12) that needs to duplicate an existing Live Document work item into multiple new work items, inserted into the same document right after the original, all in one commit (so the document gets a single new revision instead of one revision per new item).

Every approach I've tried that introduces 2+ new work items into the document's structure within a single transaction throws the same internal exception, no matter which API path I use to establish the new items' position.

Approach 1 — structure-node API (IModule.IStructureNode.moveNodeAfter):

IModule module = wi.getModule();
IWorkItem anchor = wi;
for (String[] item : splitRequirements) {
    IWorkItem target = module.createWorkItem(typeId);
    target.setTitle(item[0]);
    target.setDescription(Text.html(item[1]));
    target.save();

    IModule.IStructureNode anchorNode = module.getStructureNodeOfWI(anchor);
    IModule.IStructureNode newNode = module.getStructureNodeOfWI(target);
    anchorNode.moveNodeAfter(newNode); // position new item right after anchor
    anchor = target;
}
module.save(); // <-- throws here when 2+ new items were created above

Exception (thrown directly from Module.save()):

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Setting null owner twice!
    at com.polarion.platform.persistence.internal.pobjects.ChangeHandler.setChangeOwner(ChangeHandler.java:

A single new item (not 2+) never triggers this.

Attempted workaround A — call module.save() after every new item except the last one (so at most 1 new node is "pending" at any explicit save call): same exception, just deferred — it now surfaces as javax.transaction.RollbackException: Setting null owner twice! thrown from XATransactionService.commitTx at the transaction's commit boundary instead, proving the issue isn't when save() is called but that 2+ new nodes existed anywhere in that transaction's lifecycle.

Attempted workaround B — avoid the structure-node API entirely: instead of moveNodeAfter, splice each new item's own embed marker directly into the raw content string (module.getHomePageContent().getContent()), write it back via module.setHomePageContent(...), call module.save() once:

String html = module.getHomePageContent().getContent();
for (...) {
    IWorkItem target = module.createWorkItem(typeId);
    target.setTitle(...); target.setDescription(...); target.save();
    html = spliceMarkerAfter(html, anchorId, target.getId()); // insert "<div id=\"polarion_wiki macro name=module-workitem;params=id=PROJECT/NEWID\"></div>"
    anchorId = target.getId();
}
module.setHomePageContent(Text.html(html));
module.save();

Same exception again, this time thrown from inside setHomePageContent() itself:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Setting null owner twice!

This proves setHomePageContent() internally re-parses the content and rebuilds the structure tree, and that internal rebuild hits the identical bug once it detects 2+ new items in the diff — so the problem isn't the structure-node API specifically, it's Module.restructureNodes()/markWiChanged() itself, triggered by any path that introduces 2+ new items to an existing document's structure within one commit.

Current (only working) workaround: give every new item its own separate transaction/commit, so no single commit ever processes more than one new structure node. This works, but costs one extra document revision per new item (a 4-way split = 4 revisions instead of 1), and the operation is no longer atomic.

Question: Is there a supported Polarion SDK API for creating multiple new work items into an existing Live Document's structure within a single transaction/revision? Is this a known limitation/bug in Module.restructureNodes()/markWiChanged(), and if so, is there a tracked issue number or official workaround? (Note: duplicating an entire module into a brand-new target document, e.g. via the internal ModuleDuplicator, doesn't have this problem since every node in that case is new simultaneously — the issue is specifically about mixing new nodes into an already-persisted existing document.)

title: Why does increasing local size improve performance in OpenCL?
body:
My 1D int array represents a texture where each value is a pixel. OpenCL draws rectangles with coordinates and colors on that texture, passed from the host.

I decided to set global size to the 1D array (texture) size, and local size to 1 (as well as dimension) when calling clEnqueueNDRangeKernel. The OpenCL kernel (that represents pixels) checks if the current pixel is in the rectangle, for each rectangle. If so it draws the color. If the host passes 100 rectangles for a 1,000 x 1,000 texture there will be 1,000,000 parallel threads, each of which loops through 100 rectangles.

host.cpp:

//startup setup

size_t textureSize = textureWidth * textureHeight * 4;
size_t textureSizeCL = sizeof(int) * textureSize;

cl_mem textureCL = clCreateBuffer(context, CL_MEM_READ_WRITE, textureSizeCL, NULL, &err);

int *texture = new int[textureSize];

...

cl_mem commandsCL = clCreateBuffer(context, CL_MEM_READ_ONLY, COMMANDS_BUFFER_SIZE_CL, NULL, &err);
int *commands = new int[COMMANDS_BUFFER_SIZE];

...

clSetKernelArg(kernel, 0, sizeof(cl_mem), &textureCL);
clSetKernelArg(kernel, 1, sizeof(cl_mem), &commandsCL);
clSetKernelArg(kernel, 2, sizeof(cl_int), &textureWidth);
clSetKernelArg(kernel, 3, sizeof(cl_int), &textureHeight);

...

// loop

size_t global = textureSize;
size_t local = 1;

clEnqueueNDRangeKernel(commands, kernel, 1, NULL, &global, &local, 0, NULL, NULL);

kernel.cl:

__kernel void shader(__global int* texture, __constant int* commands, int width, int height)
{
    int id = get_global_id(0); // from 0 to width*height

    // current pixel coordinates
    int y = id/width;
    int x = id - y * width;

    int rectLeft, rectTop, rectRight, rectBottom, rectColor;

    for(int i = 0; commands[i] != STOP_CODE; i++)
    {
        if(commands[i] != NEXT_RECTANGLE)
        {
            // read rectLeft, rectTop, ...
        }
        else if(x > left && x < right && y > top && y < bottom)
        {
            texture[id] = rectColor;
        }
    }
}

It was slow. Then, without changing the kernel on the host side, I set local size to 100. 1,000 x 1,000 global work items were grouped to 10,000 local groups with 100 work items in each.

How did that make it run faster without refactoring the kernel?

title: How to open any URL in the client’s browser through CMD (Windows) running a remote SSH session (Linux)
body:
Problem

How can a Python script running on a remote Linux server open a URL in the client’s browser through VS Code Remote SSH, but same fails to open while running a remote ssh session from CMD Windows?

Note:

Its not just about a python script, in general if any program (more specifically, process) want to open browser (lets say for authentication (gcloud etc.)). It usually fails to open in CMD (having ssh session) but it works fine VSCode terminal (ssh session of the same remote VM).

Problem Description

I am connected to the same Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Linux VM through two different methods:

  • A regular SSH session using Windows CMD.

  • A VS Code integrated terminal using the Remote SSH extension.

I want to open a URL in the browser on my local Windows machine from a Python script running on the remote Linux server. Interestingly, this works differently depending on how I connect to the server.

Environment

  • Client OS: Windows

  • Remote OS: Ubuntu Linux running on a GCP VM

  • Python: 3.12

  • Connection methods: Windows CMD SSH and VS Code Remote SSH

  • Python module: webbrowser

Minimal Reproducible Example

import sys
import webbrowser


def audit(event, args):
    if event in (
        "webbrowser.open",
        "subprocess.Popen",
        "os.startfile",
        "os.system",
    ):
        print(f"[audit] {event}: {args}")


sys.addaudithook(audit)


def open_google():
    url = "https://google.com"

    try:
        controller = webbrowser.get()
    except webbrowser.Error as exc:
        print(f"No browser available: {exc}")
        print(f"Open manually: {url}")
        return False

    print("Platform   :", sys.platform)
    print("Controller :", type(controller).__name__)
    print("Name       :", getattr(controller, "name", None))
    print("Basename   :", getattr(controller, "basename", None))

    result = webbrowser.open(url)
    print("webbrowser.open returned:", result)
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    open_google()

Observed Behavior

1. Running through Windows CMD SSH

When I SSH into the VM from Windows CMD and execute the script:

No browser available: could not locate runnable browser
Open manually: https://google.com

The call to webbrowser.get() raises webbrowser.Error, so webbrowser.open() is never executed.

2. Running through VS Code Remote SSH

When I execute the same script in the VS Code integrated terminal:

Platform   : linux
Controller : GenericBrowser
Name       : /home/username/.vscode-server/cli/servers/Stable-<version>/server/bin/helpers/browser.sh
Basename   : browser.sh

[audit] webbrowser.open: ('https://google.com',)

[audit] subprocess.Popen: (
    '/home/username/.vscode-server/cli/servers/Stable-<version>/server/bin/helpers/browser.sh',
    [
        '/home/username/.vscode-server/cli/servers/Stable-<version>/server/bin/helpers/browser.sh',
        'https://google.com'
    ],
    None,
    None
)

webbrowser.open returned: True

The browser controller resolves to VS Code's browser.sh helper, and Python launches it as a subprocess.

The expected behavior is for the URL to open in the browser on my local Windows machine, rather than in a browser running on the remote Linux VM.

What I Understand So Far

Both terminals connect to the same remote VM, and the Python script executes on that VM in both cases.

However, the VS Code terminal appears to have a browser-launching configuration or integration that is unavailable in the regular SSH session.

The browser.sh helper is located inside the VS Code Server installation on the remote filesystem.

Question

title: Should this function to receive UDP packets work?
body:
In my VB app, I create a thread to read UDP packets, then send a UDP broadcast packet to request all my devices send their id info and IP address. Sending the broadcast message works and the devices respond as verified by wireshark. But the receive function gets nothing. In fact Receive never returns. I can't even use the IsCancellationRequest to end the thread because Receive blocks until it receives something. I have to manually kill the thread.

Should this function work?

  Private Shared Sub ReceiveData(token As CancellationToken)
    Using client As New UdpClient(0)
      client.DontFragment = True
      Dim anyIP As New IPEndPoint(IPAddress.Any, 2000)
      While Not token.IsCancellationRequested
        Try
          Dim data As Byte() = client.Receive(anyIP)
          Dim txt As String = Encoding.ASCII.GetString(data)
          Debug.WriteLine("Rcvd: " & txt)
        Catch ex As Exception
          Debug.WriteLine("Err: " & ex.ToString)
        End Try

      End While
    End Using
  End Sub

And here is how I am sending packets:

  Private Sub SendUDPBroadcast()
    ' Define the port you want to broadcast to
    Dim port As Integer = 2000

    ' Create the UdpClient instance
    Dim sendercient As New UdpClient()

    Try
      ' Enable the broadcast option on the socket
      senderclient.EnableBroadcast = True
      senderclient.DontFragment = True

      ' Target endpoint.
      Dim endPoint As New IPEndPoint(IPAddress.Broadcast, port)

      ' Command in a byte array
      Dim msg() As Byte = {1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0}

      ' Send the packet
      senderclient.Send(msg, msg.Length, endPoint)

    Catch ex As Exception
      Console.WriteLine("Error sending broadcast: " & ex.Message)
    Finally
      ' close the socket 
      senderclient.Close()
    End Try
  End Sub

So the answer was as Remy suggested, to use the same UdpClient to send the broadcast message and to receive the responses. There are plenty of examples where two UdpClients are used, one to send and one to receive. Regardless, using the same UdpClient for both works. Also, instead of using CancellationToken to terminate the while loop in ReceiveData, I set a 3-sec receive timeout and when the timeout exception is thrown I set boolean 'done' to true and the sub gracefully exits.
